entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Anime and the future of creativity

What makes a piece of creative work memorable? Looking to anime’s tradition of Sakuga, Territory Studio art director Erich Nemcek considers why the presence of the human hand may matter more than ever in an age increasingly shaped by automation

By Erich Nemcek 20/10/2026 3:58 am

For most animators, motion designers, and filmmakers, there are scenes they never forget. It isn’t necessarily the most expensive sequence, or the technically flawless showcase moment designed to impress an audience. More often, it’s a shot where everything suddenly feels alive through a distorted expression, or a movement so specific that it feels almost accidental. It’s the kind of moment that makes you pause and wonder who created it.

One of the more fascinating aspects of anime culture is that audiences often ask exactly that question. While most viewers leave a film discussing the story, the characters, or perhaps the director, animation fans frequently find themselves debating something far more specific: who animated that scene?

Entire communities have emerged around identifying artists through movement alone, dissecting sequences frame by frame and comparing stylistic traits in much the same way cinephiles might discuss the work of a favourite cinematographer or director.

entry.title: Digital bank Kuda targets young Nigerians with new rebrand
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Digital bank Kuda targets young Nigerians with new rebrand Working with creative agency Barkas, Kuda has developed an identity that celebrates the dreams and ambitions of the country’s youth By Daniel Milroy Maher 20/10/2026 3:50 am Copenhagen-based creative
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Digital bank Kuda targets young Nigerians with new rebrand

Working with creative agency Barkas, Kuda has developed an identity that celebrates the dreams and ambitions of the country’s youth

By Daniel Milroy Maher 20/10/2026 3:50 am

Copenhagen-based creative agency Barkas has partnered with Nigerian digital bank Kuda on a fresh identity, designed to celebrate the company’s roots, and to kickstart a new chapter of growth.

Guided by the core concept of ‘more life’ – which originates from Jamaica but is now used globally – Barkas’ work for Kuda is all about giving Nigerians the financial tools they need to spend less time worrying about money, and more time living life.

In particular, Kuda’s new identity is aimed at aspirational young Nigerians, who are digitally savvy and intentional with their money. They have strong ambitions, and they expect (and deserve) a bank that can meet them where they are.

Babs Ogundeyi, group CEO at Kuda, explains: “Life in Nigeria moves fast – it’s full of hustle, ambition and creativity, but for too long, banking hasn’t kept pace. It stopped seeing the human behind the account number and the dream behind every Naira. It stopped seeing life.”

With this in mind, Barkas created an identity that reflects the spirit of Nigeria – specifically Lagos – with all of its energy and vibrancy. Kuda’s new logo, for example, is made up of geometric letterforms that draw inspiration from Nigerian art and architecture. Barkas has also created four different iterations that can be used across various applications.

To help the brand stand out in a market that often feels cold and corporate, the design team introduced a typeface called Kuda Modena, developed by Erkin Karamemet, with the addition of a custom Naira sign to ensure it authentically represents Nigerian culture.

Following suit, the brand’s revamped photography and illustration does away with impersonal imagery and instead focuses on the people at the heart of the business – the customers. Shots by Nigerian photographer Rachel Seidu display a documentary style that helps to capture “authentic, unfiltered moments”, while the illustrations bring added warmth to the overall brand.

Finally, the team at Barkas brought all of these elements to life through motion design, helping the colours, text and imagery to pop on the screen. Employing “rhythmic editing techniques and layered sound”, the designers ensured the identity felt dynamic, and deeply tied to the idea of ‘more life’.

entry.summary: Creative Inspiration CrazyGames stakes its claim in the ‘web rush’ with bold rebrand DixonBaxi’s new work for the browser gaming platform positions it as the go-to destination for a growing global audience of players By Adam Woodward 20/10/2026 3:47 am The popular free-to-play we
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

CrazyGames stakes its claim in the ‘web rush’ with bold rebrand

DixonBaxi’s new work for the browser gaming platform positions it as the go-to destination for a growing global audience of players

By Adam Woodward 20/10/2026 3:47 am

The popular free-to-play web games platform CrazyGames has unveiled a new identity, marking its biggest evolution since its launch in 2014. Developed with DixonBaxi, whose clients in the gaming space include EA Sports and Roblox, the rebrand introduces a more prominent role for cat-eared mascot Ziggy, alongside a new tagline: ‘Your kind of crazy’.

The work arrives at a time when web gaming is gaining significant momentum, with modern technologies such as WebGL and WebGPU enabling increasingly sophisticated games to run directly in browsers. Daniel O’Kelly, VP marketing at CrazyGames, calls it “the web rush”.

By removing the need for downloads or dedicated hardware, browser-based platforms are positioning themselves as an accessible alternative to traditional gaming ecosystems. With more than 60 million monthly active users and a recorded three billion gameplays this year alone, CrazyGames will be hoping its new look cements its reputation as the home of web gaming.

The new identity aims to balance the variety of games on the platform with a consistent visual and tonal system. Ziggy, who previously had a lower profile, has been developed into a more expressive mascot that can work across the website, mobile apps, socials and merchandise, with potential for future IP extensions.

Commenting on working with GrazyGames, Marcel Jacob, head of strategy at DixonBaxi, says: “From the start, it was clear they wanted more than a new identity. What I liked was that they wanted to build a brand as fun as their games. They were open to challenging assumptions, pushing the obvious stuff out of the way and doing something actually different. That kind of drive, and the trust to make it happen, is exactly what we look for in a partner.”

The challenge for the new identity is to make CrazyGames recognisable across a vast catalogue that currently spans everything from casual puzzles to racing, action and multiplayer titles, without competing with the individual visual styles of the games themselves.

entry.title: New book celebrates the lost graphics of holiday brochures
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration New book celebrates the lost graphics of holiday brochures Holiday Exotica by Jonny Trunk is a treasure trove of forgotten travel design, from striking illustrations to delightfully offbeat typography By Adam Woodward 19/10/2026 3:23 am A chance discovery at
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

New book celebrates the lost graphics of holiday brochures

Holiday Exotica by Jonny Trunk is a treasure trove of forgotten travel design, from striking illustrations to delightfully offbeat typography

By Adam Woodward 19/10/2026 3:23 am

A chance discovery at an antiques market led Jonny Trunk down a rather niche graphic design rabbit hole. In his new book, Holiday Exotica, he explores the curious world of vintage travel brochures, whose striking use of colour, illustration and typography offer a different perspective on commercial design.

“The book started when I found a 1960s Lake District map at Spitalfields Market,” Trunk explains. “I liked the pared-back, cut-out paper graphics and thought that travel brochures, maps, leaflets, pamphlets and other ephemera might be a new old area to explore.

“The main thrust of the idea was to find something a little unusual or unexpected – odd photographic styles, strange hand drawn fonts, daring sparseness. The found brochures then went to Fuel who put them together in a book, using some and discarding others.”

The resulting collection spans a broad range of destinations and design approaches, from international and domestic tourism campaigns to airlines, car rental companies and more. Much of the material is scarce, having largely disappeared from public view due to age, making the book as much an exercise in rediscovery as a showcase of graphic ingenuity.

“I like the fact that they are quite rare,” Trunk says. “Most of them are undocumented and pretty much forgotten. They cover a fascinating breadth of styles and ideas in odd combinations. This for me was a really interesting graphic world to explore. And the only way to do that was to try and find more brochures.”

Among the highlights are a Shetland brochure featuring stained-glass-style artwork, a minimalist plan of Pompeii and a striking piece of Cornish climbing promotion. “The 1960s Pompeii plan is just a masterpiece of simplicity and tragedy, and Climbing in Cornwall took my breath away when I found it – 1960s, one photo, two colours, three worlds, bingo.

“I think the airline material is all very cool – and flying was very cool back in the 1960s and 1970s. ​​I like a lot of the English holiday brochures, with graphic ideas and photos straining to sell you a holiday here in Yorkshire. Or Camber Sands. Or on a coach to Scotland.”

For contemporary designers, the book provides a fascinating window to the past, revealing that the fundamental principles of travel advertising have remained remarkably consistent over the decades. Indeed, Trunk sees it as a vital resource of ideas that are ripe for repurposing or being applied to new work today.

“The visual grammar for these kinds of brochures hasn’t really changed since the earliest days of travel brochures – they are all selling you sunshine, sex, fun, relaxation and memories, just like today. They were just harder to make because no one had a graphic programme.

“Every graphic book I’ve made with Fuel [see also: Auto Erotica] I see very much as food. I think the graphic design world is a constantly hungry one, and these books supply a load of exciting, fresh and unseen graphic food.”

Holiday Exotica is available now via Fuel Design; fuel-design.com

entry.title: Cinematic campaign tackles railway suicides in the Netherlands
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Cinematic campaign tackles railway suicides in the Netherlands Partnering with local agency Yune, the Dutch Railway Sector and suicide prevention line 113 have created a moving film series highlighting a complex issue By Daniel Milroy Maher 19/10/2026 3:19 am
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Cinematic campaign tackles railway suicides in the Netherlands

Partnering with local agency Yune, the Dutch Railway Sector and suicide prevention line 113 have created a moving film series highlighting a complex issue

By Daniel Milroy Maher 19/10/2026 3:19 am

The Dutch Railway Sector and 113 – the national suicide prevention line in the Netherlands – have partnered with Amsterdam-based advertising agency Yune on a new campaign aimed at reducing deaths on the nation’s rail network.

Each year, nearly 200 people die by suicide on the Dutch railways, and many more people are affected by the events, including family members and friends, as well as railway staff and members of the public who experience these tragedies in-person.

Since 2010, the Dutch Railway Sector has worked with 113 on a national suicide prevention programme, but this latest campaign represents the first “joint outward communication” between the organisations.

Titled Levens tot stilstand (Lives on Hold), the campaign centres around a four-minute hero film and a six-part social series that is being rolled out across @levenstotstilstand channels. Together, these videos offer a moving insight into the lives of those contemplating suicide, and the people who are immutably affected by these decisions.

Speaking on the process of creating the films, Tim Menko, creative director at Yune, said: “The major challenge [was] translating such a fragile topic into a campaign. With [this] layered approach, we provide space to give all perspectives, from bereaved relatives to train drivers, a voice.”

The hero film follows the journey of a young man as he considers his relationship with his mother, his friends and his wider social circle, pondering whether he should share his dark thoughts with them or not. He decides that he shouldn’t burden them with his problems, and proceeds to his local train station to take his own life. The film ends with a railway worker, who is trained to identify those in need of help, approaching the man and offering him a safe space to talk, preventing a possible tragedy.

Directed by Dutch filmmaker Juul Op den Kamp, and featuring music by prominent Dutch producer Jack $hirak, the cinematic short effectively captures the feeling of helplessness experienced by those burdened with suicidal thoughts. Opportunities to share that burden with others often feel unviable, and the railway can become the final chance to turn things around – highlighting the importance of anti-suicide messaging in these spaces, and the training of workers to recognise and prevent such incidents.

Along with the social series Reality Check, which is directed by Anouk Suntjens and features ‘experts by experience’, including bereaved relatives and railway employees, the campaign films represent an important next step in making this issue a topic of national conversation. Much has already been done to prevent railway suicides, but raising awareness remains as important as ever, and compelling and anecdotal storytelling such as this offers a powerful method of engagement with the wider public.

“Over the past two years, we have worked together through a process of exceptional care, research, sensitivity and empathy for everyone who comes into contact with the topic,” said Thijs Jaski, managing director at Yune. “The shared goal and mission connect us as clients and agency: to make suicide on the tracks open for discussion and reduce the number of victims.”

entry.title: What does Britishness mean today?
entry.summary: Creative Insight What does Britishness mean today? Being challenged on a recent brief to make a brand ‘feel British’ set We Are Pi’s Rick Chant thinking about what this means, when all the clichés are removed By Rick Chant 19/10/2026 3:14 am A recent brief came with a deceptively
entry.content:
Creative Insight

What does Britishness mean today?

Being challenged on a recent brief to make a brand ‘feel British’ set We Are Pi’s Rick Chant thinking about what this means, when all the clichés are removed

By Rick Chant 19/10/2026 3:14 am

A recent brief came with a deceptively simple ambition: make the brand feel British. Properly British. Which raised a question: what is Britishness? It’s not tea or red buses and it’s definitely not Union Jacks. Britishness is tonal. It lives in understatement, irreverence and the instinct to take something sincere and immediately undermine it.

That instinct was on full display in the response to America’s all-female celebrity space jaunt featuring Katy Perry and Lauren Sánchez. An all-American moment of sincerity: big feelings, human progress and history being made. The British response? Take the piss.

Greg James, a radio DJ, asked which celebrities Britain should send into space. Within hours, his listeners had assembled the perfect crew of inappropriate familiar faces. Better still, the nominated celebrities immediately joined in. Nobody asked for a deck. Nobody needed a briefing document. There was no stakeholder alignment session. They understood the assignment: this was stupid, therefore it mattered.

entry.title: The Avalanches on the influence of childhood ads
entry.summary: Creative Process The Avalanches on the influence of childhood ads On their new album No Bad Memories, the Australian electronic outfit turn their attention to the jingles, startup chimes and commercial sounds that soundtracked their late-20th-century childhoods By Paul Weedon 16/
entry.content:
Creative Process

The Avalanches on the influence of childhood ads

On their new album No Bad Memories, the Australian electronic outfit turn their attention to the jingles, startup chimes and commercial sounds that soundtracked their late-20th-century childhoods

By Paul Weedon 16/10/2026 5:04 am

Ask Robbie Chater about the media he grew up with in 1980s Melbourne, and 40-year-old jingles instantly start playing in his head.

The ubiquitous ‘Slip, Slop, Slap’ sun-safety mnemonic that accompanied a public health campaign by Cancer Council Victoria remains firmly locked in his subconscious. Mention Australian cordial brand Cottee’s, and he instantly recalls ‘My dad picks the fruit’ – a commercial so deeply ingrained in the culture that it took on a second life as a frequent target of playground jokes. “Oh my goodness,” he beams. “It’s so evocative. I haven’t thought about that one for years, and the jingle is just embedded in my brain. It’s crazy.”

For Chater and bandmate Tony Di Blasi, the act of sampling has always been a lot like memory retrieval. But the lingering, subliminal power held by the ads of yesteryear reveals something subtle about our collective consumption of passive media. Even when we aren’t actively paying attention, these sonic motifs anchor themselves to specific chapters of our lives.

entry.title: Just Eat finds joy in staying put in VCCP campaign
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Just Eat finds joy in staying put in VCCP campaign The agency’s first campaign for the brand puts everyday moments of happiness at the heart of a new global platform, marking a shift from the celebrity-led approach By Rebecca Fulleylove 16/10/2026 3:53 am Jus
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Just Eat finds joy in staying put in VCCP campaign

The agency’s first campaign for the brand puts everyday moments of happiness at the heart of a new global platform, marking a shift from the celebrity-led approach

By Rebecca Fulleylove 16/10/2026 3:53 am

Just Eat is taking a more human approach to its advertising with Stay Just Where You Are, a new global brand platform developed by VCCP that reframes the role delivery plays in people’s lives.

The campaign centres on a simple human truth: when you’re enjoying yourself, the last thing you want to do is leave. Research cited by the brand found that 81% of people want to spend more time in the moments they enjoy. The platform shifts the focus from what Just Eat delivers to what delivery allows people to do: stay in the moment.

The hero film follows a grandfather rocking and cooing over his new grandchild. Despite having promised to cook for the wider family, he has other priorities, and makes sure a Just Eat order is on its way. Elsewhere, the campaign explores similarly absorbing and joyful moments, from friends attempting to secure festival tickets to a passionate car-park smooch, housemates playing with their cat, and a father drumming with his daughter.

The hero film was directed by Michael Spiccia through MJZ, while additional social work produced by VCCP’s Girl&Bear studio and directed by Pip + Lib.

This marks VCCP’s first work for Just Eat and a departure from the celebrity-led approach that has characterised much of the brand’s recent advertising. The long-running Did Somebody Say platform previously featured the likes of Craig David, Christina Aguilera, Snoop Dogg and Katy Perry, and helped build recognition through big names, humour and music.

While the mnemonic still appears – in updated form – at the end of the new films, Stay Just Where You Are takes a more understated approach, putting the customer’s experience at the centre of the work.

In addition to positioning delivery as a way to protect the moments people value, the campaign also signposts the brand’s offering beyond takeaway food, bringing groceries and other essentials into the same concept.

The new platform has been briefed as a long-term proposition, with global CMO Ralph Rijks describing it as the foundation for the brand’s next 20 years. Chris Birch and Jonathan Parker, joint chief creative officers at VCCP, describe the concept as “one of those lovely winged unicorns that drops out of the sky”.

To help signal this new creative direction, the launch also introduces an updated visual identity, alongside the evolved Did Somebody Say mnemonic.

entry.title: Why the future of branding is multisensory
entry.summary: Creative Insight Why the future of branding is multisensory Sensory Experiences founder Russell Jones explains how neuroscience is informing a new approach to brand design, as seen in its work with Bentley By Adam Woodward 15/10/2026 3:54 am For the most part, design is still reg
entry.content:
Creative Insight

Why the future of branding is multisensory

Sensory Experiences founder Russell Jones explains how neuroscience is informing a new approach to brand design, as seen in its work with Bentley

By Adam Woodward 15/10/2026 3:54 am

For the most part, design is still regarded as a visual business. Brands invest considerable time and effort into developing their logos, colour palettes and typefaces, whereas sound is often brought in later and the other senses are considered only when a project demands them. But what if the way a product, and by extension a brand, feels, sounds or smells could be as fundamental to its identity as the way it looks?

That is the premise behind Sensory Experiences, a research and design lab that works at the intersection of neuroscience, branding and creativity. Founded by Russell Jones, the company has spent the best part of two decades exploring how our senses influence our perception, emotion and behaviour, applying that research to the way brands think about products and consumer experiences.

Its latest work with Bentley offers a fascinating example of this. Working with the luxury carmaker on a new generation of EVs, Sensory Experiences is helping to reimagine the in-car experience through a combination of lighting, graphics, sound and haptics, forging a closer connection between driver and vehicle. The partnership, which has been developing over the past five years, also encompasses a new sonic identity, including the sound of Bentley’s electric V8 engine.

entry.title: Wildwood: The Exhibition reveals how Laika builds stop-motion worlds
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration Wildwood: The Exhibition reveals how Laika builds stop-motion worlds The Design Museum’s spellbinding behind-the-scenes show explores the practical craft and expertise within the animation studio’s work By Adam Woodward 15/10/2026 3:40 am There’s something sl
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

Wildwood: The Exhibition reveals how Laika builds stop-motion worlds

The Design Museum’s spellbinding behind-the-scenes show explores the practical craft and expertise within the animation studio’s work

By Adam Woodward 15/10/2026 3:40 am

There’s something slightly surreal about walking through a museum and suddenly finding yourself deep inside an enchanted forest. That’s the feeling evoked by Wildwood: The Exhibition, which offers a close-up look at the making of Laika’s latest stop-motion epic.

Running at London’s Design Museum, the show highlights the Portland-based animation studio’s painstaking production process, covering everything from the earliest concept sketches to the meticulously crafted miniature sets, puppets and costumes that eventually appear on screen.

Adapted from writer Colin Meloy and illustrator Carson Ellis’ 2011 novel of the same name, Wildwood draws heavily on the natural environment around Laika’s home in the Pacific Northwest. “There is so much variety of natural beauty in Oregon, we were spoiled for choice,” production designer Nelson Lowry tells CR. “I also live on the edge of Forest Park, so inspiration was five minutes away.”

In the film, the eponymous forest is treated as a character in its own right, although according to Lowry, translating nature into sets for stop-motion is tricky work. “We’ve probably all had the experience of taking a picture in a beautiful landscape to share with friends only to see in retrospect that the photo doesn’t represent our experience,” he says. “That can be a pitfall of building sets as well.

“We created models of trees and rock shapes and laid blankets over them to observe what would become the under-structure of our forest. We wanted the world of Wildwood to feel like it existed before the film and after … as if we just dropped in to tell a story. With artwork and a lot of look development (building sections of sets as tests) we attempt to build something that has that ‘wow’ factor.”

There is certainly no shortage of that here. Among the hundreds of objects on display, tiny sections of scenery reveal the astonishing amount of texture and detail that Laika packs into what might ultimately occupy only a few seconds of screen time. Elsewhere, puppet armatures expose the mechanical skeletons hidden beneath characters’ fur or skin, while assorted materials, costumes and props demonstrate the sheer volume of making that is required to capture a frame-by-frame performance.

Of course, Laika has been at this for some time now, sparking the imaginations of viewers young and old with films such as Coraline, ParaNorman, The Boxtrolls, Kubo and the Two Strings and Missing Link. After 20 years, however, Lowry says the design process is as “practiced and well-defined” as ever.

We wanted the world of Wildwood to feel like it existed before the film and after … as if we just dropped in to tell a story

“We start with references – paintings by famous landscape artists, photographs and colour ideas – I play ‘hot and cold’ with the director [Travis Knight in the case of Wildwood] and then we launch into sketches.” Once approved, the artwork effectively becomes the “bible” for the production.

Then comes what Lowry describes as his favourite stage. “We take areas of the artwork and build them as tests to be lit on stage and presented to the director in the theatre.” It’s from this moment that construction of the physical sets can begin and the film starts to take shape. For Wildwood, 136 locations were designed across 104 stages, with 49 animators working with the wider team to capture all 2,775 shots that make up the film. Meanwhile, a total of 236 puppets were created – among them a life-sized golden eagle with a five-foot wingspan.

Most of the physical design assets were digitally scanned so that Lowry and his team could easily incorporate them into the visual effects pipeline, while the larger sets were extended using VFX where building everything physically would have been impossible. Digital printing was also used for characters’ faces and some props. “Anything that gets us there is utilised,” he says.

That combination of traditional craft and cutting-edge tech is central to Laika’s appeal. Behind each fantasy world is an enormous amount of physical design and engineering. The core creative team has now worked together for nearly two decades across six films (parts of which are on display for free on the museum’s mezzanine level), and this exhibition places that accumulated expertise in full view. It is a genuinely awe-inspiring education in what it takes to create stop-motion magic on screen.

Wildwood: The Exhibition runs at the Design Museum until January 10. Wildwood is released in cinemas on October 23; designmuseum.org

entry.title: How we can become more daring
entry.summary: Creative Inspiration How we can become more daring Daring Forever is a new book by Radim Malinic which explores how we can train our brains to make changes to our lives, even if they feel risky, in order to be more creative. In the extract below he introduces the book’s core conc
entry.content:
Creative Inspiration

How we can become more daring

Daring Forever is a new book by Radim Malinic which explores how we can train our brains to make changes to our lives, even if they feel risky, in order to be more creative. In the extract below he introduces the book’s core concepts

By Radim Malinic 15/10/2026 3:22 am

Most of us have an idea of the life we want. It comes in and out of focus – sometimes we see it with acute clarity, at others, it’s more just a faint outline at the edge of our thinking. We know, somewhere beneath the noise of daily life, that we are capable of more than we are currently doing; that something is possible that we’ve not yet allowed ourselves to pursue.

And yet we wait. The common misconception is that to be daring is to be naturally gifted with such a sensibility as a personality trait, a talent distributed at birth to some more than it is to others.

But daring is about making the choice to see possibilities where you currently see limitations; to take ownership of your future rather than waiting for circumstances to rearrange themselves in your favour; to step forward before you feel entirely ready.

THE PERCEPTION PROBLEM

Comparing ourselves to others is nothing new. For as long as we have lived alongside each other, we have measured our lives against those of the people around us – our neighbours, siblings, parents, colleagues, and so on.

But now, thanks to the possibilities opened up to us through things like social media, we can compare ourselves to pretty much everyone – not just the people physically around us, who we can see, but thousands of strangers we will never meet, whose lives arrive in our hands, curated and luminous, at any hour of the day or night.

And it always seems to feel like ‘those’ people are ‘better’ than us – better jobs, better clients, bigger audiences. And in an age where tools like filters and AI are so readily available, the airbrushing and image manipulation once reserved for celebrities is now available to anyone with a phone and a few minutes to spare.

It is exhausting. And it is not reality. What we see is a carefully dressed stage, designed specifically for the world to admire. We hold their edited highlights against our unedited everything. We compare our complete experience – every frustration, setback, and unglamorous in-between moment – with the carefully selected snapshots others have chosen to show. It was never a fair comparison. It never could be.

But here’s the crux of it all, and one of the most important things for you to remember: we don’t experience life as it is, we experience it through our perception of it. The way we view the lives we have is filtered through our moods in that moment, the culture we grew up in, our fears, our unique memories (good and bad), and a thousand other things we are barely conscious of.

Most of us find ourselves caught in a paradox: we know we want things to be different, and yet we resist

Which means reality is not fixed. It moves with how you look at it. And that is one of the most liberating things you will ever understand. If the limitations you feel are not out in the world, but in the lens you’re using to see it, then shifting that lens shifts everything. The possibilities were always there – they just weren’t quite visible. That is where daring begins: with a quiet, but very deliberate, change in how you see.

THE BIOLOGY OF WHY CHANGE IS HARD

Most of us find ourselves caught in a paradox: we know we want things to be different – we sense there’s a gap between the life we’re living and the one that’s possible – and yet we resist, because something deeper and older than willpower is running in the background.

We often tell ourselves that the problem is external: we’re in the wrong job, living in the wrong city, surrounding ourselves with the wrong people. So we change the scenery and wait for everything to shift. But within months, sometimes merely weeks, the same patterns surface. The same insecurities and frustrations remain, they’re just wearing different clothes. The scenery changed, but we didn’t.

The human brain evolved to simply keep you alive, not make sure you’re happy, now, in the 21st century. And in evolutionary terms, familiarity equals safety. Repeated experiences wear neural pathways into the brain like shortcuts trodden into grass over time – the deeper the groove, the more automatically your thoughts and behaviours follow it.

Change, by contrast, demands the formation of entirely new pathways: it requires more energy, more effort, more tolerance of the unknown. And the brain, ever efficient, will resist it.

This is why wanting to change the outcome without changing the input rarely works. We want better work, deeper relationships, a more meaningful life – but we want them without having to alter our habits, perspectives, and deeply ingrained internal narratives. We are, in the most human way possible, trying to get somewhere new while insisting on using the same old map.

When we take this insight as our starting point, we can understand why well-intentioned changes so often fail to stick, and what is actually required for them to last.

Change demands the formation of entirely new pathways: it requires more energy, more effort, more tolerance of the unknown

Real change moves from the inside out. It begins with perspective – with the willingness to examine the lens before you try to change what you see through it. Because if you don’t, your brain’s hardwiring will keep returning to what it already knows, long after you’ve decided you want something different.

The question to sit with is this: if you are not willing to change, what are you choosing to accept forever? Every day spent repeating the same patterns is a quiet vote for the life you already have. To dare is to choose otherwise. It may feel like loss before it feels like growth, but that is normal – that is the work.

BECOMING MORE OF YOU

Daring is not about becoming a ‘new’ person: it’s about becoming more of who we really are. And we can only really do that by shedding the layers of ourselves that were never really ours in the first place, and finding out what remains beneath them.

In doing this, and only by doing this, you can align what you do with what actually drives you – the things that genuinely excite you, the things you’re willing to struggle for because they truly, palpably matter to you from within, not because you think they might look impressive from the outside.

There is no fixed, finished self, and so there’s no point searching for one. Instead, think of it as meeting yourself as you evolve – an ongoing process of learning, refining, and allowing. The most daring among us are simply the ones willing to show up as themselves, fully and without apology, rather than performing the version of themselves they think the world wants to see.

Because the self that needs to do the daring is the one that already exists – not a future version, not a hypothetically better one, but this one, with all its current uncertainties and imperfections and potential.

DARING NOW, AND AGAIN, AND FOREVER

Daring is a commitment – a choice you have to keep making, again and again, even when the familiar path feels like the kindest option, even when the judging brain arrives with its long list of reasons to wait. Especially then.

Many of us have histories littered with good intentions that didn’t quite take hold – half-finished projects, half-built futures, plans that began with real fervour but which quietly dissolved back into the shadows of old patterns. We shouldn’t see these as failures, but as the natural behaviour of a brain doing what brains do – returning to what it already knows.

Now that we understand that, we can learn how to work with the neurology we’ve got – your brain, your nervous system, your deeply human wiring – rather than simply trying to overcome it. It all begins with the active decision to dare. And then to dare again. Forever.

This extract is from Daring Forever by Radim Malinic, which is published on October 20 by Brand Nu Books; novemberuniverse.co.uk

Creative Insight

Why brands are rethinking packaging norms

The best packaging does more than grab attention, it shapes the experience of the product. CR explores how creatives are taking inspiration from other categories and rethinking form and function to build distinctive brands

By Rebecca Fulleylove 14/10/2026 7:53 am

Packaging has an important but difficult job. It needs to protect the product, communicate what it is and persuade people to pick it up. In a market crowded with new launches all the time, how do you make something stand out?

The skincare industry recently showed what happens when everyone tries to stand out. In September, Fenty Beauty, Glow Recipe and Huda Beauty all launched eye patches in strikingly similar twist-and-dispense tubs, despite their respective claims around innovation. Korean brand Wonder Bath had already introduced a similar format in July. As the comparisons and memes ensued, it prompted Huda Beauty founder Huda Kattan to say the brands had been “screwed over by the same packaging supplier”, which she said had misrepresented exclusivity.

Regardless of who got there first, the story highlights a tension: how do brands create something distinctive without simply following the same search for novelty? Many brands are finding answers by rethinking the physical object itself – not just how it looks, but how it works, feels and becomes recognisable over time.
